old: Formally this is supervised binary classification on a panel indexed by (station s, time t). The feature vector x_{s,t} is a function of the information available at t, written F_t; the target is y^{(h)}_{s,t} = 1[label(s, t+h) = 1]. We fit f_h(x) ≈ P(y^{(h)} = 1 | x) for each horizon, a direct multi-horizon strategy rather than a recursive one.
new: Formally this is supervised binary classification (fitting a model to labeled examples so it learns to sort new cases into one of two classes) on a panel indexed by (station s, time t). The feature vector x_{s,t} is a function of the information available at t, written F_t; the superscript in y^{(h)}_{s,t} just marks which horizon h the target belongs to, and 1[label(s, t+h) = 1] is an indicator, equal to 1 when the bracketed statement is true and 0 when it is false. We fit f_h(x) ≈ P(y^{(h)} = 1 | x), read 'the probability that y^{(h)} is 1, given x,' for each horizon, a direct multi-horizon strategy rather than a recursive one.

old: The 511 feed is an event stream sampled every 15 minutes, so incident start and end times are interval-censored. `created` is when CHP logged the report, which lags the physical event by an unknown, skewed delay.
new: The 511 feed is an event stream sampled every 15 minutes, so incident start and end times are interval-censored: we only know an incident started somewhere between two 15-minute polls, never the exact minute. `created` is when CHP (the California Highway Patrol) logged the report, which lags the physical event by an unknown, skewed delay.

old: The dot product equals |x||w|cos θ, so it measures alignment. The set of points where w·x + b = 0 is a line or a plane, which is the decision boundary of a linear model.
new: The dot product also equals |x||w|cos θ, where |x| and |w| are the two vectors' lengths and θ is the angle between them, so it measures alignment: largest when two vectors point the same way, near zero when they meet at a right angle, negative when they point opposite ways. The set of points where w·x + b = 0 is a line or a plane, which is the decision boundary of a linear model.

old: Schemas and keys: a primary key identifies a row, a foreign key links tables, an index makes lookups fast. Types matter: store timestamps as timestamps, not text.
new: Schemas and keys: a primary key is a column, like `station_id`, whose value is unique for every row, so it identifies exactly one row; a foreign key is a column in one table that stores another table's primary key value, which is what `JOIN` matches on. A database index is a lookup structure built on a column so the database can jump straight to matching rows instead of scanning every one, a different thing from a pandas DataFrame's index (its row labels) despite the shared name. Types matter: store timestamps as timestamps, not text.

old: Query execution: how a planner turns SQL into scans, joins and aggregates, why indexes help lookups but not scans, and how to read an `EXPLAIN` plan. Transactions and ACID guarantees; concurrency and isolation levels in one paragraph.
new: Query execution: how a planner turns SQL into scans, joins and aggregates, why indexes help lookups but not scans, and how to read an `EXPLAIN` plan, which prints the plan's steps without running the query. A transaction groups several reads and writes into one all-or-nothing unit; ACID names what it guarantees, atomic (all or nothing), consistent (never leaves the data breaking its own schema), isolated (concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-finished work), and durable (once committed, a crash can't undo it). An isolation level controls how strictly 'isolated' is enforced, trading correctness against speed; DuckDB and this course's file-based pipeline mostly sidestep the question, since one program reading files nobody else is writing to at the same time has nothing to isolate.

old: The trick is a self-join: the same table of (station, timestamp, speed, occ) is merged back onto `df` under a different name. First `df` is merged with the registry to gain the neighbor id column; then `nb`, a renamed copy of the current readings, is merged on (neighbor id, timestamp), so each row picks up its neighbor's reading at the same moment. The `rename(columns=...)` calls give the new columns names such as `down1_speed` (first downstream neighbor's speed) and `up1_occ`; the odd slicing expression inside just shortens 'upstream' to 'up' and 'downstream' to 'down'. Same timestamp, so nothing from the future is used.
new: The trick is a self-join: the same table of (station, timestamp, speed, occ) is merged back onto `df` under a different name. First `df` is merged with the registry to gain the neighbor id column; then `nb`, a renamed copy of the current readings, is merged on (neighbor id, timestamp), so each row picks up its neighbor's reading at the same moment. The `rename(columns=...)` calls give the new columns names such as `down1_speed` (first downstream neighbor's speed) and `up1_occ`. Inside that rename, `side[:2 if side=='upstream' else 4]` is a conditional expression tucked inside a slice: Python first works out `2 if side=='upstream' else 4`, which is `2` when `side` is `'upstream'` and `4` otherwise, and only then applies `side[:that number]` to cut the word short, giving `'up'` or `'down'`. Same timestamp, so nothing from the future is used. After running this, check `df.down1_speed.isna().mean()` and `df.up1_speed.isna().mean()`: most rows should have a real number, since most stations have a neighbor; a value near 1.0 means the merge keys do not match, usually a wrong id type or a registry that failed to load.

old: Alternatives keep more information: regress the speed ratio with a pinball loss and derive probabilities from quantiles; or model episode onset as a point process with covariates and predict hazard. Both avoid the brittle 3-step run and make horizon coherence natural.
new: Alternatives keep more information: regress the speed ratio with a pinball loss and derive probabilities from quantiles; or model episode onset as a point process, a model of when events happen along a timeline, with covariates, the input features that shift how likely an event is, and predict hazard, the instantaneous risk of an episode starting right now given none has started yet. Both avoid the brittle 3-step run, and both make horizon coherence natural: a single underlying model of the continuous process, rather than three separately-trained 15/30/60-minute classifiers, cannot contradict itself across horizons the way three independent binary models sometimes do.

old: The ratio `speed / profile_speed` says how the current speed compares with typical: 1.0 is normal, 0.5 is half speed. `is_slow` is 1 where the ratio is below 0.6, stored as `float32` so that NaN can survive in it. Then the run rule: a slow episode needs three consecutive slow rows, so that one noisy reading does not count. `rolling(3).sum()` adds each row's value to the two before it within each station (`groupby("station_id")` keeps the window from crossing stations); a sum of 3 means three slow rows in a row. `reset_index(level=0, drop=True)` strips the extra group level that rolling adds so the result lines up with `df` again; `== 3` makes the boolean; `astype("int8")` stores it as a one-byte integer. The sort before rolling matters: rolling reads rows in table order, so the table must be in time order within each station.
new: The ratio `speed / profile_speed` says how the current speed compares with typical: 1.0 is normal, 0.5 is half speed. `is_slow` is 1 where the ratio is below 0.6, and 0 otherwise (a row whose profile is missing also lands on 0, since a comparison against a missing value is never true); it is stored as `float32`, a number rather than a plain true/false, because the next line sums three of these values together, and summing needs numbers, not booleans. Then the run rule: a slow episode needs three consecutive slow rows, so that one noisy reading does not count. `rolling(3).sum()` adds each row's value to the two before it within each station (`groupby("station_id")` keeps the window from crossing stations); a sum of 3 means three slow rows in a row. `reset_index(level=0, drop=True)` strips the extra group level that rolling adds so the result lines up with `df` again; `== 3` makes the boolean; `astype("int8")` stores it as a one-byte integer. The sort before rolling matters: rolling reads rows in table order, so the table must be in time order within each station.

old: Linear regression minimizes the sum of squared errors; with several clues it is y ≈ w·x + b, fit by least squares. Metrics: MAE (robust, in mph), RMSE (sensitive to outliers), MAPE (percent, undefined at zero), R² (fraction of variance explained). Residual plots show where the model fails.
new: Linear regression minimizes the sum of squared errors. With one clue it's the familiar y ≈ a + bx; with several clues at once, each one gets its own weight, and the prediction is y ≈ w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + ... + b, written compactly as y ≈ w·x + b, where w·x (a dot product) just means multiply each weight by its matching clue and add up all those products. Fitting the line means choosing every weight and b by least squares, the same idea as before, just with more numbers to choose at once. Metrics: MAE (robust, in mph), RMSE (sensitive to outliers), MAPE (percent, undefined at zero), R² (fraction of variance explained). Residual plots show where the model fails.

old: Clustering as optimization (k-means as coordinate descent on within-cluster variance; Gaussian mixtures and EM as its probabilistic version), the meaning of a 'good' clustering (no ground truth; stability and downstream utility), and the curse of dimensionality for distances. PCA as the best low-rank approximation (Eckart-Young), its relation to the SVD, and its limits (linear, variance is not always signal). Nonlinear reduction (t-SNE, UMAP) for visualization only.
new: Clustering as optimization: k-means turns out to be a form of coordinate descent that minimizes within-cluster variance, and a Gaussian mixture fit with EM is its probabilistic, soft-assignment version. There is no ground truth to check a clustering against, so a 'good' clustering is judged by stability across reruns and by whether it helps a downstream task instead. Distance-based methods like k-means also run into the curse of dimensionality: with enough features, every pair of points ends up looking almost equally far apart, which weakens what 'nearest' even means. PCA is the best possible low-rank approximation of the data in a precise sense (the Eckart-Young theorem), it is closely related to the singular value decomposition (SVD), and its real limit is that it only ever looks for linear structure, so variance along a curved or nonlinear pattern is not something PCA can see as signal. Nonlinear techniques like t-SNE and UMAP exist for exactly that gap, but only for visualization: they preserve which points were close neighbors well enough to plot, not the kind of well-defined axes PCA produces, so their output should never be fed into another model as a feature.

old: Forward pass: h = ReLU(W₁x + b₁), p = σ(w₂·h + b₂). Loss: cross-entropy. Backward pass: ∂L/∂w₂ = (p − y) h; ∂L/∂h = (p − y) w₂; through ReLU multiply by 1 where the pre-activation was positive and 0 elsewhere; ∂L/∂W₁ = δ₁ xᵀ.
new: Forward pass: h = ReLU(W₁x + b₁), p = σ(w₂·h + b₂). Loss: cross-entropy. Backward pass: ∂L/∂w₂ means how the loss L changes for a tiny nudge to w₂ alone, everything else held fixed, the same idea as dy/dx but for a function of many weights at once. ∂L/∂w₂ = (p − y) h; ∂L/∂h = (p − y) w₂; through ReLU multiply by 1 where the pre-activation was positive and 0 elsewhere, giving δ₁, the hidden layer's own error; ∂L/∂W₁ = δ₁ xᵀ.

old: Layers: convolution (filters, stride, padding), nonlinearity, pooling, batch normalization, then fully connected layers or global pooling. Why convolutions: weight sharing and locality make them data-efficient and translation-equivariant. Classic architectures (LeNet, AlexNet, VGG, ResNet with skip connections) and what each added.
new: Layers: convolution (filters, stride, padding), nonlinearity, pooling, batch normalization, then fully connected layers or global pooling. Why convolutions: weight sharing (the same filter is reused at every position) and locality make them data-efficient and translation-equivariant, meaning a pattern learned in one part of the image is recognized anywhere else it appears, without learning it separately for each spot. Classic architectures (LeNet, AlexNet, VGG, ResNet with skip connections) and what each added.

old: The training pipeline: pretraining on web-scale text, supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, preference tuning (reinforcement learning from human feedback or direct preference optimization). Scaling laws: loss falls predictably with model size, data and compute. Inference: sampling, temperature, context windows, cost per token.
new: The training pipeline: pretraining on web-scale text, supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations people wrote, and preference tuning, adjusting the model using which of two answers people preferred (reinforcement learning from human feedback and direct preference optimization are two ways to do this). Scaling laws: loss falls predictably with model size, data and compute. Inference: sampling (picking words from the model's predicted probabilities rather than always the top one), temperature (a knob for how much randomness that sampling uses), context windows (how much text the model can read at once), and cost per token.

new: Adaptation: prompting (instructions, few-shot examples, structured output), parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA), retrieval (embeddings, a vector index, chunking), and tool use. Evaluation: held-out benchmarks, task-specific test sets, and human review. new: Feature extraction versus fine-tuning; learning rates for pretrained layers; catastrophic forgetting, losing an old skill while learning a new one because the same weights get overwritten. Self-supervised objectives: masked prediction, contrastive learning (pull similar views together), next-step prediction. new: FastAPI: define request and response models, add an endpoint (one URL the server answers, like `/predict`), run with a server (a program that stays running and listens for requests instead of exiting after one command), read the auto-generated docs. Docker: a Dockerfile lists the base image and install steps, `docker build` and `docker run` package and run it, `.dockerignore` keeps data out. old: Memory rules: float32, categorical ids, monthly Parquet parts, one heavy job at a time, three gigabytes kept free. Scheduling rules: launchd plists with `StartInterval`, Energy settings set to never sleep, `caffeinate` around the long download.
new: Memory rules: float32, categorical ids, monthly Parquet parts, one heavy job at a time, three gigabytes kept free. Scheduling rules: launchd plists with `StartInterval`, Energy settings set to never sleep (in System Settings, under Battery or Energy Saver, turn off 'put hard disks to sleep' and set the machine to never sleep on power), `caffeinate` around the long download (run `caffeinate long_running_command`, which keeps the Mac awake only until that one command finishes).

old: Markov decision processes: states, actions, transitions, rewards, discounting. Value functions and the Bellman equation; Q-learning and policy gradients as the two families; exploration versus exploitation; deep RL (a network for the value or policy). Bandits: epsilon-greedy, upper confidence bound, Thompson sampling. Simulators are usually required because trying actions in the real world is expensive or unsafe.
new: A Markov decision process names the pieces: states (the situation right now), actions (what the agent can do), transitions (how the state changes after an action), rewards, and discounting (caring a little less about reward that arrives later). A value function estimates the total future reward available from a state, and the Bellman equation is the rule that a value equals the reward right now plus the discounted value of whatever comes next; Q-learning learns those values directly and picks the action with the highest one, while policy gradients instead adjust the policy itself to get more reward, the two main families. Exploration versus exploitation is trying something new against using what already works; deep RL just means a neural network stands in for the value function or the policy once there are too many states to write down. Bandits, the one-decision case, choose when to keep exploring with epsilon-greedy (mostly pick the best-known option, occasionally pick at random), upper confidence bound (favor options you are still unsure about), or Thompson sampling (pick each option in proportion to how likely it is to be the best one). Simulators are usually required because trying actions in the real world is expensive or unsafe.

old: Fairness definitions and why they conflict: equal error rates across groups, calibration within groups, demographic parity; you cannot have all at once. Measuring: slice every metric by area and time. Privacy: anonymization fails against linkage; differential privacy adds calibrated noise with a provable guarantee; aggregation thresholds and k-anonymity are weaker but common. Ethics in practice: documentation (datasheets, model cards), stating limits, and a person accountable for decisions.
new: Fairness definitions and why they conflict: equal error rates across groups, calibration within groups, demographic parity (the model alerts the same share of people in every group); you cannot have all at once. Measuring: slice every metric by area and time. Privacy: anonymization fails against linkage, where someone combines an 'anonymous' record with outside information to identify a person; differential privacy adds calibrated noise with a provable guarantee (a mathematical limit on how much any one person's data could have changed the released numbers); aggregation thresholds (never publishing a count below some minimum) and k-anonymity (making sure every published row looks like at least k others) are weaker but common. Ethics in practice: documentation (datasheets, model cards, short standard write-ups of what a dataset or model is and is not good for), stating limits, and a person accountable for decisions.

old: Matrix factorization with implicit feedback, nearest-neighbor methods, and modern two-tower models that embed users and items; candidate generation then ranking; ranking losses (pointwise, pairwise, listwise). Metrics: precision at k, recall at k, mean average precision, NDCG. Offline evaluation is biased by what was shown (exposure), which is the central difficulty.
new: Matrix factorization with implicit feedback (clicks and views instead of star ratings), nearest-neighbor methods, and modern two-tower models that embed users and items so a good match ends up a short distance apart; candidate generation (cheaply shortlisting a few hundred possible items out of millions) then ranking (scoring that short list carefully); ranking losses (pointwise: score each item alone, pairwise: get one pair in the right order, listwise: get the whole list in the right order). Metrics: precision at k, recall at k, mean average precision, NDCG (normalized discounted cumulative gain, which rewards good items for being near the top of the list, not just present in it). Offline evaluation is biased by exposure, since the log only shows what the old system already chose to show, so items it never showed have no data to judge.

For traffic, METR-LA and PEMS-BAY are the standard datasets, METR-LA being 207 loop detectors in Los Angeles and PEMS-BAY being Bay Area PeMS with 325 sensors, and the metrics are MAE, RMSE and MAPE at 15, 30 and 60 minutes. old: The Hessian H of a function f(w) is the matrix of its second partial derivatives, Hᵢⱼ = ∂²f/∂wᵢ∂wⱼ, capturing how the slope changes in every direction at once. If H is positive semidefinite everywhere (vᵀHv ≥ 0 for every vector v), the function is convex, meaning it has a single bowl shape with no separate local dips to get stuck in. Newton's method updates parameters using both the gradient and the Hessian, w ← w − H⁻¹∇f(w), which accounts for curvature and can converge in far fewer steps than gradient descent on well-behaved (locally quadratic) functions. For logistic regression, the loss's Hessian is Xᵀ diag(p(1−p)) X, which is positive semidefinite, proving the loss is convex and gradient descent is guaranteed to find the global minimum.
new: The Hessian H of a function f(w) is the matrix of its second partial derivatives, Hᵢⱼ = ∂²f/∂wᵢ∂wⱼ, capturing how the slope changes in every direction at once. If H is positive semidefinite everywhere, meaning it never curves downward no matter which direction v you check (vᵀHv ≥ 0, where vᵀ just means v written as a row instead of a column so the multiplication lines up), the function is convex, meaning it has a single bowl shape with no separate local dips to get stuck in. Newton's method updates parameters using both the gradient and the Hessian, w ← w − H⁻¹∇f(w), where H⁻¹ is the Hessian's matrix inverse, undoing what multiplying by H does, the way dividing by a number undoes multiplying by it, which accounts for curvature and can converge in far fewer steps than gradient descent on well-behaved (locally quadratic) functions. For logistic regression, the loss's Hessian is Xᵀ diag(p(1−p)) X, which is positive semidefinite, proving the loss is convex and gradient descent is guaranteed to find the global minimum.

old: Plain gradient descent updates each parameter as w ← w − η∇L, where η is the learning rate; Adam instead keeps a running average of the gradient, momentum, and of the squared gradient for every parameter, and updates using both: θ_t = θ_{t−1} − α·m̂_t/(√v̂_t + ε), where the hats denote bias-corrected averages. This gives each parameter effectively its own adaptive step size, parameters with noisy, small gradients get relatively bigger steps than under plain gradient descent. AdamW adds weight decay as a separate term subtracted directly from the weights each step, rather than folding it into the gradient the way old-style L2 regularization did, which matters for how well the regularization actually works.
new: Plain gradient descent updates each parameter as w ← w − η∇L, where η is the learning rate; Adam instead keeps a running average of the gradient itself, call it m, and of the squared gradient, call it v, for every parameter, and updates using both: θ_t = θ_{t−1} − α·m̂_t/(√v̂_t + ε), where θ_t is the parameter after step t, α is the learning rate (the same idea as η above, just a different letter), m̂_t and v̂_t are those two running averages with a small correction for the fact that they both start at zero, and ε is a tiny number added only so the division never blows up if v̂_t happens to be zero. This gives each parameter effectively its own adaptive step size, parameters with noisy, small gradients get relatively bigger steps than under plain gradient descent. AdamW adds weight decay as a separate term subtracted directly from the weights each step, rather than folding it into the gradient the way old-style L2 regularization did, which matters for how well the regularization actually works.
